newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Swedish farm minister fights for food safety.
newsitem.headline: Swedish farm minister fights for food safety.

text.p: Stricter measures, such as compulsory beef labelling, are needed to improve food safety and protect consumers from mad cow and other deadly diseases, Swedish agriculture minister Annika Ahnberg said on Tuesday.

Ahnberg, whose appointment as minister coincided with a crisis over bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), said Sweden was the first country to call for EU labels showing where cattle were born, raised and slaughtered.
Britain, where BSE was widespread, sparked the crisis by admitting that the disease could be linked to a deadly human equivalent called Creutzfeldt-Jakob-Disease (CJD).
Initially only Germany and Austria backed beef labels but over the past 12 months there has been a complete change of attitude towards food safety and consumer protection, she said.
"Now it's very important, there's pressure on countries to protect consumers but there's still not enough change," Ahnberg told Reuters in an interview.
Ahnberg was in Brussels for a monthly meeting of EU farm ministers with beef labelling the main issue.

Sweden has strict animal health and food hygiene standards and has waged a major campaign to eradicate salmonella bacteria in poultry. It says it is free of BSE and scrapie, a similar brain wasting disease in sheep.

Pressure for action has increased after EU veterinary inspectors recently reported serious weaknesses in member states in BSE detection and controls, suggesting that the disease may have been under-reported on the European continent.
Farm ministers have been criticised for putting the interests of the beef industry before public health.
EU countries must improve BSE detection methods, scientific research and controls, said Ahnberg, 48, a Social Democrat.
"We don't know if we are at the start of a catastrophe, how it's spread," she said, noting new evidence of hygiene problems in slaughter houses.
Asked about prospects for the EU lifting a worldwide ban on British beef exports, Ahnberg said Britain must first show it had fully implemented all the pre-conditions.
"I don't know how long this will take," she said cautiously.
The BSE crisis pointed to the need for further reform of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) to improve food quality and bring production and demand into balance, Ahnberg added.

Sweden, where farmers form only two percent of the workforce, wants to scrap export subsidies, payments to farmers to set aside farmland and purchases of surpluses into public stores and lower prices towards world levels.
Small farmers in northern Sweden and elsewhere in Europe would be supported by enhanced payments to develop alternative small businesses and tourism in rural areas.
But generous EU subsidies for wealthy southern Swedish farmers were difficult to defend.
"It's unacceptable to pay so much money for something which doesn't work," said Ahnberg, a former communist. "The system is getting more and more complicated but not protecting consumers."
Despite her criticism of EU farm policy, Ahnberg is described as "pragmatic" and "pro-EU" by her entourage.
But apart from Britain and Denmark, the Swedish call for reforms is likely to fall on deaf ears in EU farm meetings.
